groups.title: Advice on family visit
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: Advice for a family visit to the city.

transcript.text: Sandra, I seem to remember you had some family visitors staying with you recently
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, that's right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: My brother and his family were here a couple of months ago.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: OK, good.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well, I wanted to ask for your advice.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I've got my cousin and her family visiting next month and as I don’t have kids, I’ve no idea where to take them.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: What about accommodation?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Are they going to stay with you in your flat?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: No, thankfully.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: There wouldn’t be room.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: My cousin wants me to recommend a hotel.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Do you know anywhere?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yes, I do actually.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I always recommend people stay at the King’s Hotel.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Where’s that near?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s about a five minutes walk from Murray Station, so nice and central.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It’s actually on George Street.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh yes, I know.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I think they’re on quite a tight budget, so how much roughly is it to stay there?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: If you book a family room, it’s about £125 per night.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: My brother paid for two double rooms in the end, and I think that was around £95 for each room.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh, that’s not too bad.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So how old are your cousins’ kids?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Twelve and nine.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: So I want to organise some trips while they’re here.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I was thinking of doing a bus tour of the city centre, as none of them have been here before.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Those bus tours are quite expensive.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I think it’s better to do a walking tour.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It gives you a much better feel for the city.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: There’s one that starts from Colton Square.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It takes a couple of hours and doesn’t cost that much.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sounds good.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’ll look that up.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: If the weather’s nice, one thing you could do is visit the old fort.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You could get there by boat.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: The whole trip takes half a day.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s a really good idea.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’d like to do that myself.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And if the weather bad I was thinking they could go to the science museum.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: But maybe they could do that when I'm at work.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah don't forget it closed on Mondays
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: They're here from Saturday for four nights so Tuesday would be best I think
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And it won’t be so crowded then.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Saturdays are terrible.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I took my kids to the exhibition on old computers there and it was far too crowded.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I wanted to go back but it’s finished now.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s a shame.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: My cousin’s kids would have enjoyed that.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: There’s another one starting soon on space, which looks really good too.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: OK, well, I’ll mention that to my cousin.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Have you thought about where to take them to eat?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I really like all the food stalls at Clacton Market.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: My cousin’s vegetarian.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I know it’s one of the best places for that kind of food.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Definitely, and there’ll be loads of choices for the kids too.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You need to get there quite early, though.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: At the weekend, most of the stalls stop serving lunch at 2.30.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Good point.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s all going to need careful planning.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: My cousin said she’d love to take the kids to a show at the theatre, but tickets are so expensive.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I know.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: But you can get some good deals if you book online with bargaintickets.com for the following day.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: On some seats there's a 75% discount
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Really.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I must try and get some
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah There are lots of things you can do for free as well.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: No need to spend a fortune.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Like what?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: They’re coming next month, right?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, check and see if it’s the same weekend as the Roots Music Festival in Blakewell Gardens.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: R-O-O-T-S?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, check it out online.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It’s always a family-friendly event and there’s no entry charge.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That sounds perfect.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And if you’re in Blakewell Gardens, climb Telegraph Hill.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You’ll be able to look right down on the port.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Everyone’s always really impressed because it’s so huge.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh yeah, I’ve been meaning to do that for ages.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’ve heard the view’s amazing.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, it’s really worth the effort.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, that’s given me loads of ideas.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Thanks so much.
transcript.speaker: MAN

parts.context: A stadium guide describes family activities and football history.

transcript.text: Good morning and welcome to City Football Club.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’d like to give you some useful information about your visit to the stadium today and then we’ll start the tour of the areas of the stadium that are open to visitors.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I can see lots of children here today, so just to let mums and dads know a few things before we start.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The stadium has lots of stairs and the players’ tunnel is very dark.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Please don’t let your children wander off on their own, even for a minute.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We don’t want any accidents or anyone getting frightened.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Cameras are permitted everywhere and you can take pictures of your child shooting a penalty.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Assistants are helping to organise this and hopefully the queue won’t be too long.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s very hot and sunny out on the pitch today.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You can get food and drink at the cafe and I really recommend the healthy lunch boxes for children Also in the cafe, children are invited to do a football drawing.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We pick the best one at the end of the afternoon.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So don’t forget to put your name and contact details on the back.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That way if you’ve left the stadium before then, we’ll send your prize, but sadly we can’t return drawings.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’d like to mention some features of the tour.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ll start with the 360 cinema experience, which has been very popular over the years, and then I’ll take you to the players’ dressing rooms, before going outside to the seating area and the pitch.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I should say, if you’d prefer your visit to be self-guided, please collect headphones from the reception, and then you can listen to the pre-recorded information at your own speed.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve only just introduced this feature and would appreciate your feedback.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re thinking of offering tours in other languages in future, so if you have any thoughts on that, we’d welcome those too.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you plan to return another time, you might like to book one of our VIP tours.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ve only just started offering these and they can be booked online.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, the stadium you see today was built in 1989 as part of a three-year redevelopment project.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: While that project was going on, the team had to play its matches at the ground of another club.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Apart from that, the club has been here on this site since 1870.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As some of you may know, that was the start of a really important decade in the history of football in this country.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: For example, 1870 was also the year that football teams started to include a player whose role it was to guard the goal.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s hard to imagine what the game must have been like without someone in that position, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1872 and 73, many other clubs were established, both here and abroad.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And the following year, in 1874, referees were allowed to send players off if they committed certain offences.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And also in that year, teams started having to swap ends at half-time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: One fact I was interested to discover was that in early football games the aim was for the scorer to get the ball between two flag posts and later between sticks joined at the top with a piece of tape.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1875, that tape was replaced with the solid crossbar that we’re familiar with today. 1877 saw the founding of further new clubs and the history books tell us that in the same year all the clubs decided to set a limit of 90 minutes for each match Before that it was a more casual arrangement and this sometimes caused huge arguments and sometimes fights during matches when one team called the end of the game and the other team wanted to play on to try and score a winning goal.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: By 1878, the number of teams in the Football League increased again.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In addition, referees started using whistles and electric lamps were installed on certain pitches.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This was a significant change, as games could then be played in the evenings all year round.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In 1880, clubs began to charge fans for admission to games, even though players were still amateurs and had other proper jobs.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s hard to imagine in the modern professional game. where top players earn significant sums of money from both playing and commercial activities.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

groups.title: Teaching handwriting
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

parts.context: Two students discuss handwriting and learning.

transcript.text: How are you getting on with the assignment on handwriting?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Not too bad.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You know, I hadn’t realised that children benefit in so many ways from learning to write.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It’s such an important skill, and yet most people think handwriting is less important than in the past, because people hardly ever write by hand these days.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, and all the evidence suggests children should learn to write by hand before they learn to type, not least because it helps their memory.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: The physical act of writing helps children to remember letters.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That seems pretty obvious when you think about it.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: What’s less obvious is how it helps develop their concentration.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: They have to sit still and focus on one thing.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, that aspect of handwriting had never occurred to me before.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Same here.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’m not sure I understand how it improves children’s imagination, though.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well there was that study which showed that primary age children generated more ideas when they were writing by hand than using a keyboard I would have guessed that would be the case.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Hmm yeah I never associated spatial awareness with handwriting either.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I thought spatial awareness was more to do with knowing where you are in relation to objects or other people.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I thought that too.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: But good spatial awareness is essential for writing because you have to space words correctly.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It’s not just fine motor skills that improve through writing, as I’d always assumed.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Handwriting is so much harder for children with dyspraxia, who have problems coordinating movement.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s good there are lots of things you can do in the classroom to help them.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: They need so much more support with letter formation.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: You need to play lots of games to help them distinguish letter shapes.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It takes a lot of patience.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, I like the idea of using one of those pens that lights up if you press too hard.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That seems like a really simple solution.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, absolutely.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’m not sure there’s much you can do about children with dyspraxia writing very slowly.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s more important to focus on accuracy and as they get more confident, I think they eventually speed up.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: One quite simple thing you can do is to use grid paper.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So they write each letter in a box and that trains them to space the letters correctly.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Indeed, that’s more important for legibility than trying to get them to write in a straight line.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: For some children, it might be better to teach them to write on a laptop rather than by hand, like children with dyslexia.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: They often really struggle with handwriting and some just give up.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yeah, it’s not as frustrating for them if they get things wrong.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: On a keyboard, they can be more willing to have a go.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: But I read that developing fluency isn’t any faster.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Did you read that article on the benefits of teaching print rather than cursive handwriting, where the letters are joined up?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, in the past, cursive writing was certainly considered more stylish and educated, but not anymore.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Teachers’ attitudes have changed because it’s been proved that cursive is more difficult to learn, especially for children with learning difficulties who find joining up letters really challenging.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I agree.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I was always worried that my poor handwriting affected my exam results, and now research shows that I was right to worry.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’m sure a lot of students think it’s unfair that they’re being judged on their handwriting, not just their knowledge.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Marks are definitely affected if examiners can't read the script.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That is why it has always been so important to teach children to write legibly.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Do you think the role of handwriting will change in the future?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I can’t see that changing much.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Touch typing still isn’t taught in most schools, which is a shame.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: But maybe that won’t be necessary in the future, because people will also be able to write by hand on digital devices.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Anyway, teachers understand the value of handwriting.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s a basic life skill.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: True.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: However, the fact is that people are writing by hand less and less and relying on digital devices.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That does cause some problems.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: You mean like note-taking.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: There are lots of apps for that.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And for reading historical documents, apparently.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: But my mum is shocked by my awful spelling and the fact that my punctuation is really inconsistent.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I think you can put that down to lack of practice.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I expect so.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Personally, I miss writing by hand.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I hardly ever write anything now.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I remember my grandparents had such beautiful handwriting and it was so individual.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Nobody I know would be able to identify my handwriting now.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s a shame.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I know.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I feel the same way.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I used to write a diary by hand and now I do that digitally.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It just seems less effort to do it that way.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: So it’s not just a problem…
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

groups.title: Research around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

parts.context: A lecture about birds of prey near the Chembe Bird Sanctuary.

transcript.text: We’ve been looking at different types of conflicts that may arise between wildlife and humans at the boundaries of protected areas, such as national parks and animal sanctuaries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: I’d like to illustrate this by telling you about some research that I’ve been involved in recently in the Central African country of Zambia in the area around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary which contains over 300 of the listed birds of Zambia These include a number of birds of prey such as eagles hawks and owls that live by hunting and killing other birds and animals Now most of the people living in the local communities near to the bird sanctuary are small-scale farmers and these birds of prey provide important social and ecological benefits to them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, a lot of damage can be caused to farmers’ crops by rodents, such as rats, which would consume the crops as they grow in the fields, as well as after harvesting if they weren’t hunted and killed by the birds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And the predatory habits of these birds also protect farmers in other ways.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal, and birds of prey have a major role in keeping their populations under control.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Local people have always been aware of these benefits and for years, even before the sanctuary was opened in 1973, the birds played a key role in the culture of the region.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, more recently, the sanctuary and its birds have also become increasingly important to the community in economic terms, because at present, after a relatively slow start, tourism has become an important source of revenue for them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, although these birds of prey are protected by the government, their numbers are falling.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some of these deaths are accidental.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Fatalities occur when birds alight on roads to catch and eat their prey, and are hit by fast moving traffic.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Drivers in Zambia have to take special care at night, as birds may regard the quieter roads as safe places to sleep.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Accidental deaths may also occur if these birds fly close to high power lines as they may be electrocuted.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is a particular danger in the heavy rain which can occur in the region in the months from December to April.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And local farmers also pose a threat to these birds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As well as growing crops, small-scale farmers in the area also rear chickens.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These provide food for the farmers’ families, as well as being an important source of income.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But they’re also an easy target for birds of prey, and so farmers may shoot these birds, which is illegal but understandable, or they may poison the birds, which again is illegal and can have negative effects on the ecosystem.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So how else can farmers protect their chickens from birds of prey?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some people believe that to prevent the predators from settling near the area where the chickens are kept, it’s best to keep this area free from vegetation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But in fact, this is counterproductive, as it means the chickens have no cover to hide in and they’ll be easier for the birds to see.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another possibility would be to prevent the chickens from going outside at all and to keep them safe from predators inside a building, but this would cost far too much to be a practical solution.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Nearly all the farmers reported that they spent a lot of time and effort trying to frighten off the birds of prey without actually harming them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Most of the farmers had at least one dog and said this was a big help at scaring away the predators.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Some of the farmers also reported that during the breeding season, when the chickens were particularly vulnerable, they encouraged their children to watch over the chickens and to hit pans with a metal spoon so that the resulting noise would succeed in driving away birds that were trying to seize the young chicks None of these methods was 100% effective so as a result the village people told us that rather than just using one method, they were forced to use a combination for them to have any effect.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And even so, these birds of prey remain a major threat to the chickens’ survival and cause considerable economic loss to farmers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So we looked at the possibility of a longer-term solution to…
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
